planting.note: Germinate seed in a cool, 55-65F greenhouse or alpine frame, then transplant container-grown youngsters outdoors after last frost into a cool-summer microclimate.

directions: Espeletia pycnophylla, the frailejon, is a slow-growing Andean paramo rosette plant that eventually develops a thick, insulated trunk topped by a crown of silvery, densely hairy leaves adapted to intense high-altitude sun, nightly frost, and near-constant fog. In cultivation it needs a cool, frost-light climate with mild summers rather than hard freezes or sustained heat, which is why it is grown outdoors mainly in cool coastal gardens such as those in the San Francisco Bay Area, and elsewhere as a container or alpine-house specimen. Give it full sun, sharply drained volcanic or rocky soil, and regular moisture without standing water, reflecting a habitat with frequent misty precipitation but excellent natural drainage. Growth is extremely slow even for a long-lived perennial, so treat it as a multi-decade architectural collector's plant rather than a quick-maturing garden subject.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online
San Francisco Botanical Garden plant records

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, sheltering young trees from harsh wind until established.

directions: Polylepis australis, the quenoa or tabaquillo, is a small, gnarled Andean tree famous for forming the highest-elevation native forests in the world in its native Argentina and Bolivia, and for its thick, papery, cinnamon-red bark that peels in multiple curling layers as added cold insulation. In the garden it is grown chiefly as a slow-growing specimen for its sculptural, twisted trunk and fine, fern-like, pinnately divided foliage rather than for its small, inconspicuous flowers. It prefers full sun, deep well-drained soil, and a cool-temperate to montane climate, tolerating considerable cold once established but appreciating shelter from harsh wind while young. Because wild seed can be hard to source reliably, most gardeners start with container-grown nursery stock from specialist tree growers.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Set out container-grown stock in spring in an essentially frost-free climate; this species comes from New Caledonia's ultramafic maquis and needs mild winters year-round.

directions: Araucaria rulei is a strikingly columnar New Caledonian conifer endemic to the island's ultramafic maquis, where it grows on nutrient-poor, metal-rich, serpentine-derived soils that few other large trees can tolerate. Its stiff, blue-green, awl-shaped leaves are densely packed along upswept branches, giving mature trees a tight, almost bottlebrush silhouette distinct from the broader-crowned araucarias more commonly grown. It is cultivated only in essentially frost-free, mild coastal climates similar to its home island, and performs best in full sun on sharply drained, lean soil. Because it is slow-growing and still uncommon outside botanical and specialist conifer collections, source seed from specialty exotic-conifer seed suppliers rather than conventional nurseries.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online
IUCN Red List — Araucaria rulei species assessment

planting.note: Set out container-grown stock in spring in a frost-free, mild coastal climate; this species naturally grows on sea cliffs and ultramafic outcrops in southern New Caledonia.

directions: Araucaria luxurians grows wild on coastal cliffs and rocky ultramafic outcrops in southern New Caledonia, making it one of the most salt- and drought-tolerant araucarias grown. Young trees have a dense, symmetrical, pyramidal habit clothed in soft, flattened, bright-green juvenile foliage, while older trees develop the more open, tiered branching typical of large araucarias along with firmer, scale-like adult leaves. It needs a frost-free to nearly frost-free climate and full sun, and its natural tolerance of lean, mineral-rich, well-drained coastal soils makes it a good choice for exposed seaside plantings in suitably mild regions. As with other New Caledonian araucarias, availability is limited mainly to specialty exotic-conifer and palm-and-cycad seed suppliers.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online
IUCN Red List — Araucaria luxurians species assessment

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade after frost danger has fully passed; this species is more cold-sensitive than the common sago palm.

directions: Cycas seemannii is a robust Pacific island cycad native to New Caledonia, Vanuatu, and Fiji, where it grows in maquis, savanna, and open forest margins, including nutrient-poor ultramafic sites. It develops a stout, often solitary trunk topped by a crown of long, stiff, dark-green pinnate leaves, giving it a bolder, larger-scale presence than the common sago palm, Cycas revoluta. Like other cycads it is extremely slow-growing and essentially trouble-free once established, tolerating drought, poor soil, and salt-laden coastal air. Grow it in full sun to light shade in sharply drained soil in warm, frost-free to nearly frost-free climates, and source plants or seed from specialty cycad and palm nurseries, since it remains uncommon in general garden-center trade.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online
The Cycad Pages / International Cycad Society species accounts

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun once frost danger has fully passed; it needs an essentially frost-free climate.

directions: Metrosideros laurifolia, known as laurel ohia, is a New Caledonian myrtle adapted to the island's harsh ultramafic maquis, where it tolerates mineral-poor, heavy-metal-laden soils that few other shrubs can colonize. It carries unusually large, thick, leathery, glossy leaves, often with reddish leaf stalks, on a dense evergreen shrub or small tree, topped with the typical Metrosideros display of red, bottlebrush-like flower clusters. In cultivation it wants full sun to light shade, sharply drained, lean soil, and a frost-free to nearly frost-free climate, performing best where summers are warm and winters stay mild. Because it remains a specialty item outside botanical collections, source seed from rare-plant seed houses rather than conventional garden centers.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online
